groupOverview.headline: Computing research from the social edge inward.
groupOverview.body: The Third Space research group, led by Prof. Ishtiaque Ahmed at the University of Toronto, studies the social, ethical, and political dimensions of computing and artificial intelligence. The group works at the intersection of human-computer interaction (HCI), AI, and critical computing to understand how technologies shape—and are shaped by—everyday life practices, particularly in contexts of marginalization and global development, centering communities that are often overlooked in mainstream computing research.

professor.name: Prof. Ishtiaque Ahmed
professor.title: Associate Professor
professor.bio: Ishtiaque Ahmed is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at the University of Toronto and serves as Associate Director of the Knowledge Media Design Institute (KMDI). He is also affiliated with the University of Toronto's iSchool, Data Sciences Institute, School of the Environment, School of Cities, Institute of Health Emergencies and Pandemics, Acceleration Consortium, and Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society. In addition, he serves on the University of Toronto's Research Ethics Board (REB) and AI Task Force. Beyond the University of Toronto, he has served as the National AI Consultant for Bangladesh with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and is a member of the MIT Global Humanities Initiative.
professor.researchInterests: Ishtiaque's current research focuses on AI safety, AI governance, AI policy, ethical and responsible AI design, and human–AI interaction. He designs AI tools and services aimed at addressing global challenges in health, sustainability, and peace in a responsible and accountable manner. His work critically examines the ethical foundations of AI systems and explores community-based, participatory approaches to AI development. His research is primarily published in HCI venues such as CHI, CSCW, FAccT, ICTD, DIS, and COMPASS, as well as AI venues including ACL, EACL, ECIR, AAAI, and WWW.

about.title: About the Group
about.body: Through empirical and design-oriented research, the group develops and studies socio-technical systems that support more responsible, participatory, and context-aware forms of AI and digital technologies. Their work is grounded in collaboration with communities and draws on interdisciplinary perspectives to reimagine how computing systems can better serve diverse human values and needs.

team.pageBody: The Thirdspace group brings together faculty, postdocs, PhD students, graduate students, and undergraduates who study the social, ethical, and political dimensions of computing and AI.

members.name: Farhan Samir
members.title: NSERC Postdoctoral Fellow
members.focus: Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto
members.bio: Farhan Samir is an NSERC Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Computer Science at the University of Toronto. He completed his PhD in linguistics at the University of British Columbia, focusing on computational methods for knowledge representation and information systems. His research studies representational imbalances in large information systems, especially Wikipedia, and designs AI methods to audit and expose these gaps.
members.researchInterests: Farhan studies representational imbalances in large information systems, especially Wikipedia, and designs AI methods to audit and expose these gaps. He co-developed InfoGap, a dual-model AI method that identifies facts present in one language's Wikipedia page but missing or differently presented in another.

members.name: Dipto Das
members.title: Postdoctoral Fellow
members.focus: University of Toronto / Cornell University
members.bio: Dipto Das is a postdoctoral researcher whose work bridges AI, algorithmic accountability, and socio-technical systems. He examines how AI systems and online platforms shape decision-making, public discourse, and identity across varied cultural contexts. His research covers AI governance, context-sensitive fairness measures, and cultural/political dimensions of AI usage.
members.researchInterests: Dipto's research covers three threads: Governing (studying policies, impact assessments, AI registries and procurement for accountability), Evaluating (context-sensitive fairness measures and benchmarks for low-resource languages), and Situating (cultural/political dimensions of AI usage, including identity, moderation, and diaspora practices).

members.name: Rachel Levine
members.title: Arts & Science Postdoctoral Fellow
members.focus: Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto
members.bio: Rachel F. Levine is a cultural anthropologist and postdoctoral fellow in U of T's Computer Science Department. Her work examines the ethics of human-AI relationships, especially the normative and emergent aspects of humans forming bonds with robotic pets. She draws on anthropology to explore technology's social role.
members.researchInterests: Levine studies how people form meaningful relationships with robotic pets, and how these reveal broader conceptions of intelligence, care, and companionship. Her project examines design, production, and use of robotic pets in contexts like home care and therapy.

members.name: Ramaravind K M
members.title: PhD Candidate
members.focus: Faculty of Information · University of Toronto
members.bio: Ramaravind is a Ph.D. candidate in the Faculty of Information, a graduate fellow of the Data Sciences Institute (DSI), and a graduate affiliate of the Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society (SRI) at the University of Toronto. He is co-advised by Prof. Ishtiaque Ahmed and Prof. Shion Guha. He is a member of the Department of Computer Science's Third Space research group, the Dynamics Graphics Project lab, and the iSchool's Human-Centered Data Science Lab.
members.researchInterests: Ramaravind's research centers on the dual reasoning challenge in AI safety: focusing on both how AI practitioners reason about their own assumptions and decisions, and how LLMs exhibit reasoning-like behaviors in safety-critical contexts. He develops reflective frameworks to surface implicit practitioner assumptions and designs theoretically grounded methods to evaluate LLM reasoning with greater depth than existing benchmarks allow. Situated at the intersection of HCI and NLP, his research combines user studies with insights from sociopolitical and philosophical theories to examine the normative and ambiguous dimensions of AI safety.

members.name: Salman Sayeed
members.title: PhD Student
members.focus: Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto
members.bio: Salman Sayeed is a natural language processing (NLP) and HCI researcher focused on social and educational AI. He joins U of T in Fall 2026 as a PhD student under Prof. Ahmed. He currently leads AI engineering at a major Bangladeshi telecom.
members.researchInterests: Sayeed's research aims to make AI systems more ethical and inclusive. He focuses on social AI agents in education, designing AI-driven pedagogical conversational agents that help teachers create educational content.

members.name: Md. Arid Hasan
members.title: PhD Candidate
members.focus: Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto
members.bio: Md. Arid Hasan is a PhD student in the U of T CS department and a graduate fellow at the Schwartz Reisman Institute. His research advances human-centered, responsible AI, especially NLP for global health contexts and low-resource languages.
members.researchInterests: Hasan studies how large language models encode cultural and subjective knowledge across languages and contexts. A key focus is on AI for mental health, investigating how culturally-aware AI can support community health workers in Global South settings.

members.name: Sheza Munir
members.title: PhD Student
members.focus: Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto
members.bio: Sheza Munir is a PhD researcher in U of T's Computer Science Department, advised by Dr. Ahmed. She holds a Master's in Health Informatics from University of Michigan. Her work focuses on the sociotechnical aspects of data annotation and AI model evaluation.
members.researchInterests: Munir's research sits at the intersection of NLP and sociotechnical systems. She studies data annotation as a human practice: how annotator identity, expertise, and experience influence what data gets labeled or ignored.

members.title: PhD Student
members.focus: Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto
members.bio: Zarif Masud is a PhD student in the Department of Computer Science at the University of Toronto, working on topics related to data migration and information retrieval systems.
members.researchInterests: Zarif's research focuses on how information retrieval systems construct and amplify immigration narratives, and the role of artificial intelligence in immigration from automation to accountability.

members.name: Yasaman Rohanifar
members.title: PhD Candidate
members.focus: Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto
members.bio: Yasaman Rohanifar is a PhD candidate in U of T's Computer Science Department, supervised by Prof. Ahmed. She holds a Master's in Health Informatics and a BSc in CS (both U of T). Her research bridges HCI and financial technology.
members.researchInterests: Rohanifar studies how emerging digital systems (like FinTech apps) influence people's everyday financial decisions, risk perceptions, and vulnerabilities. She approaches financial technology from a human-centered perspective.

members.name: Maryam Mokhberi
members.title: PhD Candidate
members.focus: Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto
members.bio: Maryam Mokhberi is a PhD candidate in U of T's CS Department, supervised by Prof. Ahmed. She applies HCI and design to empower marginalized communities, with a focus on inclusive AI assistance for immigrant-led nonprofit organizations.
members.researchInterests: Mokhberi studies how digital and AI infrastructures affect immigrant-led nonprofit and community activities. She developed AMINA, an AI assistant to help immigrant organizations navigate funding and outreach.

members.name: Priyank Chandra
members.title: Assistant Professor
members.focus: Faculty of Information, University of Toronto
members.bio: Priyank Chandra is an Assistant Professor in the Faculty of Information at U of T, where he directs the STREET Lab (Socio-Technical ResistancE and Ethical Technologies Lab). His research centers on technology and marginalized communities, focusing on social movements, worker resistance, and accessibility.
members.researchInterests: Chandra studies socio-technical practices of marginalized and informal communities, such as worker organizations, disabled communities, and social movements. He applies interdisciplinary theories from sociology, STS, and development studies to design interventions that support these communities.

members.name: Aparna Moitra
members.title: Former Postdoctoral Fellow
members.focus: Ulula (Canada) / University of Toronto
members.bio: Aparna Moitra is an ICTD/HCI researcher focusing on technology in development contexts, especially gender justice. She was a postdoctoral researcher in Prof. Ahmed's Thirdspace Lab at U of T, studying online feminist movements and ICT for gender-based violence.
members.researchInterests: Moitra studies how ICT tools can empower marginalized groups, particularly women and LGBTQ+ communities in South Asia. She has worked on designing culturally-appropriate digital safe spaces and voice-based social media for low-literacy contexts.

members.name: Mohammad Rashidujjaman Rifat
members.title: Former PhD Student · Now Asst. Professor
members.focus: University of Notre Dame
members.bio: Mohammad Rifat is an Assistant Professor of Tech Ethics & Global Affairs at the University of Notre Dame. He earned his PhD in CS from U of T (2025) under Prof. Ahmed. His research spans HCI, ethics in AI, and critical social sciences, focusing on the ethics of computing in pluralistic societies.
members.researchInterests: Rifat's work focuses on the ethics of computing in pluralistic societies. He investigates challenges of cultural and value diversity in AI, designing systems that support plural ethics and promoting pluralistic practices.

members.name: Dina Sabie
members.title: Former PhD Student · Now Professor
members.focus: Humber College, Toronto
members.bio: Dina Sabie is a technologist and designer studying migration and resilience. She holds a PhD in Computer Science from U of T (Ahmed lab) and currently teaches game programming at Humber College. Her dissertation examined the emotional dimension of migration and how digital tools can support migrants' resilience.
members.researchInterests: Sabie's dissertation focused on the emotional dimension of migration, exploring how migrants use digital devices and augmented reality to participate in resilience activities and maintain community ties.

members.name: Hazem Ibrahim
members.title: Former MSc Student · Now PhD Candidate
members.focus: New York University
members.bio: Hazem Ibrahim is a PhD candidate in Computer Science at New York University, specializing in computational social science and human-AI interaction. He earned an M.Sc. at U of T (2020). His research examines how algorithms create systematic inequalities.
members.researchInterests: Ibrahim studies systematic biases in large-scale data systems. His work includes algorithmic audits of social media and analyzing media representation.

members.name: Abdul Kawsar Tushar

members.focus: UserTesting, Toronto
members.bio: Abdul Kawsar Tushar is a software engineer with experience in ML and HCI. He earned an M.Sc. in CS at U of T (2018-2020), specializing in HCI under Prof. Ahmed.
members.researchInterests: Tushar's graduate research involved improving OCR for HCI and developing classification techniques.

aboutPage.headline: Studying computing from the margins inward.
aboutPage.subhead: Founded and led by Prof. Ishtiaque Ahmed at the University of Toronto, Thirdspace is a research group that studies the social, ethical, and political dimensions of computing and artificial intelligence.
aboutPage.heroSubParagraph: Thirdspace is a research collective at the University of Toronto reimagining how AI and digital systems can be designed alongside — not for — communities shaped by marginalization, displacement, and grassroots care.
aboutPage.heroResearchPostureBody: Critical, empirical, and participatory — we treat every technology as a question of power, and every design as an act of accountability.
aboutPage.missionBody: Through empirical and design-oriented research, we develop and study socio-technical systems that support more responsible, participatory, and context-aware forms of AI and digital technologies — particularly with communities too often left outside the room where technology is designed.
aboutPage.approachBody: We combine long-term fieldwork with iterative system design, partnering with community organizations, public institutions, and grassroots groups across the Global South and Canadian margins. Our research brings together ethnographic inquiry, interviews, co-design workshops, and the development of working prototypes to create technologies grounded in lived experiences.

approachItems.title: Empirical Inquiry
approachItems.body: Conducting ethnography, interviews, and field studies to understand computing through everyday life practices and situated experiences.

approachItems.title: Participatory Design
approachItems.body: Working with communities as collaborators and co-creators, rather than treating them as passive subjects of technological development.

approachItems.title: Critical Computing
approachItems.body: Examining the social, ethical, and political implications of AI and digital infrastructures, and questioning how technology shapes power, access, and everyday life.

aboutPage.storyBody: Thirdspace sits at the intersection of human-computer interaction, AI, and critical computing. The group is housed in the Department of Computer Science at the University of Toronto and is affiliated with several cross-disciplinary labs and initiatives across the university. Our work has been supported by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC), the National Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR), and partner organizations across the Global South.

contact.headline: We'd love to hear from you.
contact.body: Whether you are a prospective student, research collaborator, journalist, or community partner, we welcome you to connect with us. We aim to respond to inquiries within a few working days.
contact.connectBody:
We welcome inquiries from prospective graduate students, visiting researchers, and community partners interested in our work. Due to the volume of requests, we may not be able to respond to every message, but we carefully review each inquiry.

For graduate admissions, please apply through the University of Toronto's Department of Computer Science and indicate your interest in working with Prof. Ahmed's group in your statement of interest.
